slides.text:
Rust code is made of statements and expressions. A statement does something and gives no value. An expression gives a value.

`let n = 5;` is a statement. The `5` inside it is an expression.
A block `{ ... }` is an expression too. Its value is its last line, as long as that line has no semicolon.

exercises.title: A block with a value
exercises.guide: Give a variable the value of a whole block.

chunks.guide: The block is an expression: the last line, with no `;`, is the value it gives.

notes.text: The whole block becomes the value of the variable.
No semicolon: this is the value of the block.

exercises.title: Prepare, then freeze
exercises.guide: Use a mutable variable inside a block to prepare a value that stays fixed outside.

chunks.guide: `s` lives only inside the block. The last value it holds is what `speed` receives, and `speed` is not mutable.

notes.text: Changes the variable before the block ends.

exercises.title: Finish the block
What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: The block runs when `a` is defined, so it prints `b is 7` first and hands back 7. Then `a is 7` prints.

exercises.title: A discounted receipt
exercises.guide: Apply a discount inside a block, shadowing the price only there.

chunks.guide: The block discounts the price, adds shipping and gives the total.

notes.text: A new price, visible only until the block ends.

chunks.guide: Print the original price, then the total.

slides.text: A `let` is a statement: it gives no value, so it cannot sit where a value is expected. In a block, the lines before the last are statements that run in order. The last one, with no `;`, is the value.
A semicolon turns an expression into a statement and throws its value away. The calculation still runs, but nothing is kept, and rustc warns about the unused result.

exercises.title: A block as an argument
exercises.guide: A block can stand anywhere a value is expected.

chunks.guide: A value to read inside the block.
The block sits where `println!` expects its value, and gives what its last line holds.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `n * 10;` ends with a semicolon, so its value is thrown away. The block gives the last line, `n + 1`.

exercises.title: Finish the score
The empty value
exercises.guide: Compare a block with a final value and one that ends in `;`.

chunks.guide: Both blocks hold a `4`. Only the second one has a semicolon after it.

notes.text: The block gives (), a value that means nothing.

chunks.guide: Print both with the debug format, which can show `()`.
Two more blocks with other names: this one ends with its value, the other with a semicolon.

notes.text: The semicolon makes the block give ().

exercises.title: The bill that vanished
exercises.guide: Trace the side effect and the value of each block, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `bill` runs its block: the `println!` prints `subtotal 36` right away. The last line `subtotal + 4;` has a `;`, so 40 is thrown away and `bill` holds `()`. `tip` ends with `rate` and holds 5.
